Hi everyone,  I am currently working on my Master's thesis and conducting a study on Artificial Intelligence in video games. As a gamer, I want to gather real feedback from the community on how AI behaviors impact our gaming experiences.  **Purpose of the Survey & Abstract:** The primary purpose of this research is to evaluate how players perceive and interact with Artificial Intelligence and Non-Player Character (NPC) behaviors in video games. While AI has become an integral component of modern game design, its presence is often most effective when it operates seamlessly in the background. This study aims to analyze the sociological and technological implications of this "invisible" AI integrated into digital entertainment. Specifically, the research explores how elements such as procedural content generation and complex NPC behavioral patterns affect player immersion, emotional engagement, and overall gameplay dynamics. By gathering quantitative and qualitative data directly from the gaming community, this thesis seeks to bridge the gap between technical AI development and the actual user experience, providing deeper insights into what players truly value in virtual interactions.  **Research Institute:** University of Catania — Master's Degree in International Cooperation.  **Researcher Contact Data:** Author: Mirko Moschella Email: [Mirko.moschella@gmail.com](mailto:Mirko.moschella@gmail.com)  The survey is completely anonymous, consists of multiple-choice and short-answer questions, and will take about 3 to 5 minutes to complete.  [https://forms.gle/aJUdtr4DzADiguheA](https://forms.gle/aJUdtr4DzADiguheA)     Have you recently played a game where an NPC's behavior completely broke your immersion, or conversely, made the world feel incredibly alive? What specific mechanics caused that reaction? I would love to read your thoughts in the comments!

Rotating shifts and limited free time mean my gaming sessions are pretty unpredictable - sometimes 30 minutes, sometimes a free evening. I used to think my backlog problem was "too many games, can't decide what to play." But looking back at what actually stops me from returning to games, it's almost always the same thing: after a 2-3 week gap in a story-driven game, I've lost the thread of what was happening, and re-entering feels like starting from scratch mentally - so the game just stays untouched.  I think this gets less attention than the "choice paralysis" narrative, but for people with limited or irregular time it might actually be the bigger issue. Curious whether others notice the same pattern, or whether choice paralysis really is the main blocker for you.

Hi everyone,  I’ve been reflecting on the evolution of the MOBA genre, specifically the early hybrid attempts before titles like *Smite* or *Paragon* entered the market. One specific game that always comes to mind is Land of Chaos Online (LOCO), published around 2010.  Mechanically, the game deeply engaged a specific niche. The combination of tactical hero-brawler elements with a third-person perspective felt ahead of its time. However, the game ultimately failed. From an analytical perspective, the reasons seem obvious on the surface  Severe Economy Inflation: The in-game currency systems fractured rapidly  Aggressive Pay-to-Win Mechanics: Character progression and power spikes were heavily tied to monetization, even in the "Evolution" of the game.  Difficult Balancing: fighting PvP with overpowerd gear   Despite these fatal flaws, the core gameplay loop possessed an undeniable appeal that modern MOBAs rarely replicate in the same way.  For those who played it or studied the genre during that era:  What specific design elements or mechanical choices do you think made the core gameplay so captivating despite the terrible publisher decisions?  Do you believe the "Third-Person Action-MOBA" hybrid failure was purely due to poor execution (monetization/balancing), or is there an inherent flaw in combining fighting-game/brawler mechanics with traditional MOBA map strategy?  Looking forward to your design-focused insights.

When people talk about worldbuilding in platformers, Mario usually gets dismissed as pure nonsense: floating bricks, singing clouds, turtle kings and plumbers jumping on mushrooms. But if you actually stop and think about it, the Mushroom Kingdom is surprisingly honest with its own madness. The original manual explicitly said Bowser transformed the citizens into blocks, pipes connect underground plumbing, and the whole place operates on fairytale logic. It's a cohesive psychedelic dream. It doesn't pretend to be an actual functioning society with urban planning, so your brain just accepts it.  Then you look at Sonic. And Sonic's world is an existential nightmare if you think about it for more than three seconds.  Sonic games want you to believe these places are either pristine natural paradises (Green Hill), ancient ruins, or cities inhabited by actual humans who pay taxes and commute in traffic. Yet somehow, every single cliffside features a giant dirt loop-de-loop perfectly carved out of the terrain, floating corkscrews, and mechanical booster pads bolted directly onto ancient grass.  Who built these massive red springs in the middle of a tropical beach? Did prehistoric civilizaitons construct an entire highway system exclusively catered to a blue hedgehog doing 700 mph, centuries before he was even born? Eggman builds machinery, sure, but half of these obstacle courses are just sitting in the wilderness, waiting for someone to launch off a ramp into the stratosphere.  It feels like the ultimate case of mechanics completely obliterating worldbuilding. Mario built a fantasy playground where the rules are absurd but consistent. Sonic constantly tries to ground its world with cities, lore, and drama, while forcing you to ignore that its geography looks like a Hot Wheels set vomited over an archipelago.

I appreciate "hard fights" in gaming.   It doesn't have to be a literal fight, something like having to spend minutes thinking about a chamber in Portal 1/2 and doing some trial and error, slowly figuring things out until finally succeeding would count.   Indeed, a certain level of friction is needed for it to feel satisfying.   Too little and it "doesn't feel good" (My issue with the first two bosses of "Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth", though it does improve later), too much and you don't even feel like giving it a shot.   But where is the fuzzy line in the middle? Where is the edge between one and the other?  It's easy to say "I GIVE UP!" and then come back the next day or after a small pause and then succeeding, I had such experiences when trying to get S-Rank on the Archery Challenge for "Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth" or defeating the last boss of the Normal Ending of "Cave Story+" (CS+ is one of those games that seem to fit that one "This game sucks/This game is awesome" Mario 64 gif).   But when should you ACTUALLY give up?  Once again using Cave Story+ as an example, I didn't even try to platinum it because I was sure that if I had trouble normally, then I would have no chance at Hard Mode, so I didn't even feel bad about it.   What made me write this thread was my experience with the Boss Rush mode of "Astalon: Tear of the Earth". While the Normal Mode has the issue of bosses not feeling fulfilling to beat since at the point you fight them you're so overpowered that they're trivialized, boss rush is based around beating the six game bosses with minimum upgrades.   I wouldn't say I haven't improved since I started trying it (At first I had around a 40% success rate at beating the very first boss and never went further than the second, now it's around an 80% success rate and I even went as far as the third boss), but my troubles at the second boss on things I haven't even seen guides mentioning might signal that I just might not have the reflexes needed to beat it.  If CS+ Hard Mode was something so beyond my skills that I didn't even feel bad for not trying it, Astalon is in a sort of "uncanny valley" of difficulty where it all feels so familiar that it makes me think "I should be able to do this" while also seeming above my skill level.  So I wanted to hear the opinions of others: When is it worth to keep mining because diamonds might just be ahead, and when should you put your pickaxe down?

I've been thinking quite a bit about ARC Raiders' introduction of a PvE-only matchmaking option, and I believe there's a much larger discussion worth having here. One that extends well beyond ARC Raiders itself and raises some uncomfortable questions about creative integrity, player entitlement, and the increasingly blurred line between responding to community feedback and fundamentally compromising a game's identity.  At what point does accommodating players who dislike a game's core mechanics become a disservice to those who purchased and enjoyed the game specifically because of those mechanics?  And perhaps more importantly, what kind of precedent does it establish when a sufficiently persistent section of a community can convince developers to fundamentally reconsider the type of game they created?  For context, Embark's PvE toggle is currently a limited test running October 13–20, not a confirmed permanent addition. I recognize that distinction. My concern is less about this particular test than what its potential permanence could signify for multiplayer game development.  ---  A game should not have to abandon its identity to accommodate people who dislike its genre  ARC Raiders was released, marketed, and sold as a PvPvE extraction shooter.  That's not some obscure technical classification. It's the foundation of the experience.  The uncertainty of encountering another player, the possibility of cooperation or betrayal, the tension of carrying valuable loot while knowing another human being could take it from you, and the constant decision-making surrounding risk versus reward are fundamental to what makes extraction shooters work.  The possibility of hostile player interaction isn't an unfortunate inconvenience attached to the gameplay. It IS part of the gameplay.  Remove that uncertainty, and you've fundamentally altered the experience, even if the maps, enemies, weapons, and objectives remain identical.  An encounter with another Raider is compelling precisely because you don't know what will happen. Are they friendly? Are they bluffing? Should you cooperate? Should you avoid them? Is that stranger approaching you because they need help, or because they've decided your equipment belongs to them?  These situations cannot be replicated through AI encounters alone, because their defining characteristic is the unpredictability of human behavior.  A friendly interaction has substantially more meaning when hostility was a genuine possibility.  If everyone is mechanically prevented from attacking one another, cooperation ceases to be a meaningful decision involving trust and vulnerability. It becomes the default condition.  That's a fundamentally different social dynamic.  There's nothing inherently wrong with wanting a cooperative shooter. Plenty of excellent games provide exactly that experience.  But why should an established PvPvE extraction shooter be expected to transform itself to accommodate people who fundamentally dislike the PvP component they knowingly purchased?  ---  "Just let people play how they want."  This is easily the most common defense of PvE-only modes, and superficially, it's difficult to disagree with.  Who doesn't support player choice?  The problem is that this argument treats multiplayer game design as though it's a collection of isolated personal experiences, where one person's choices exist independently of everyone else's.  They don't.  In a shared multiplayer ecosystem, player behavior, matchmaking populations, progression systems, resource availability, and social interactions are interconnected.  Consider what happens if a substantial portion of the cooperative or risk-averse population migrates to PvE-only servers.  The remaining PvPvE population potentially becomes disproportionately populated by players primarily interested in combat.  That changes the composition of encounters for everyone remaining.  The uncertainty that made the original experience compelling could gradually disappear, replaced by an increasingly predictable environment where practically every player interaction results in immediate hostility.  Ironically, introducing a mode intended to accommodate peaceful players could make the original mode considerably less socially diverse.  And the argument that people should simply play whichever mode they prefer fails to address that consequence.  The original experience may still technically exist, but the ecosystem responsible for producing that experience has changed.  This isn't merely hypothetical concern about separate playlists. "Embark itself acknowledges" (https://arcraiders.com/news/pve-toggle-beta-test) potential consequences for matchmaking quality, queue times, the player economy, and the tension the game was designed around.  They've introduced reduced loot values and restrictions on certain map conditions to mitigate those concerns, which is sensible. But the need for those safeguards illustrates the underlying point:  Adding an option to a multiplayer game is not necessarily a neutral decision.  Sometimes expanding one player's freedom changes another player's experience.  And that deserves considerably more scrutiny than simply declaring that additional options are always beneficial.  ---  "But the PvPvE mode still exists. Nobody is taking anything away from you."  This argument confuses the continued existence of a game mode with the preservation of the experience that made it appealing.  Imagine a multiplayer survival game whose appeal revolves around scarcity, player conflict, and difficult decisions regarding trust.  Now introduce an alternative environment where players can gather resources without the possibility of hostile encounters, potentially transferring some of those resources or progression advantages back into the original ecosystem.  Even if progression is carefully balanced, you've changed the incentive structure governing how players interact with the game.  And even if progression is entirely separated, you've divided the population that previously participated in a shared set of circumstances.  The game isn't simply two independent products that happen to share an executable. Both modes compete for players, development resources, balancing attention, and future content priorities.  The claim that an optional mode cannot affect players who never select it ignores how multiplayer ecosystems actually function.  A mode can remain selectable while becoming meaningfully different from the experience people originally purchased.  That's precisely why I find the "nobody is forcing you to play it" argument so unconvincing.  Nobody needs to force you into the new mode for its existence to have consequences for the original one.  ---  "If people want PvE, why shouldn't developers listen to their community?"  Developers absolutely should listen to feedback.  But there's an enormous difference between improving a game within its established design philosophy and changing that philosophy to satisfy people who dislike it.  Better matchmaking? Absolutely.  Stronger anti-cheat systems? Essential.  Addressing exploitative spawn camping, improving onboarding, balancing equipment, and making combat encounters more understandable? All worthwhile discussions.  Removing an entire category of player-driven risk, however, is a fundamentally different proposition.  Not every complaint reflects a problem that should be solved.  Sometimes the discomfort a player experiences is an intentional consequence of the genre.  A horror game isn't necessarily poorly designed because someone finds it frightening. A survival game isn't fundamentally defective because someone dislikes resource scarcity. A competitive fighting game isn't obligated to remove adversarial combat because some players find losing stressful.  Those characteristics aren't incidental obstacles standing between the player and the intended experience.  They're part of what defines that experience.  A player disliking a mechanic does not automatically mean the mechanic is failing at its intended purpose.  And importantly, purchasing a game does not entitle someone to demand that its developers reconstruct the experience around their individual preferences.  You're entirely entitled to dislike PvP, avoid extraction shooters, criticize their mechanics, or request alternatives.  But the developers are equally entitled to maintain the creative identity of the product they chose to make.  There's an important distinction between listening to your community and allowing your community to dictate the fundamental design philosophy of your game.  ---  "Wouldn't PvE attract more players and make the game more successful?"  Possibly. And this is probably the strongest argument in favor of the change.  Embark has published data suggesting substantial interest in cooperative play, including 51% of surveyed players expressing interest in a dedicated PvE option.  That deserves acknowledgment. It would be intellectually dishonest to pretend this interest comes exclusively from some insignificant handful of vocal players.  But popularity alone does not answer whether a particular design decision is beneficial.  There's a meaningful distinction between making a game appealing to more people and making a game better at delivering the experience it was designed to provide.  Those two objectives frequently overlap, but they aren't interchangeable.  A tactical shooter could theoretically attract a broader audience by reducing its tactical complexity. A hardcore survival game could attract additional players by eliminating resource loss. A competitive racing simulator could become more approachable by simplifying its handling model.  But at what point do those accommodations diminish the very qualities responsible for attracting the original audience?  Not every game needs to appeal to everyone.  In fact, some of gaming's most memorable experiences exist precisely because their developers were willing to commit to a particular vision, even when that vision was inherently unappealing to certain audiences.  There's also the practical issue of development resources.  Supporting a separate PvE experience can eventually create pressure for distinct progression systems, enemy balancing, content pacing, endgame activities, and additional mechanics necessary to keep that audience engaged.  Those resources have opportunity costs.  More players might justify that investment, but increased accessibility and commercial potential are not automatically proof that the original design is being improved.  Commercial viability and creative integrity aren't inherently mutually exclusive. But they aren't necessarily synonymous, either.  ---  "ARC Raiders was originally supposed to be a PvE game anyway."  Yes, and I think this is an important historical detail.  ARC Raiders began development as a cooperative PvE experience before Embark substantially reworked the project into a PvPvE extraction shooter.  But an abandoned development concept is not the same thing as the finished product that was ultimately released and sold.  Plenty of games underwent dramatic transformations during development.  What matters in this discussion is the experience Embark ultimately chose to build, market, and release, and the systems and community that developed around it.  Its original conception doesn't automatically establish that returning to PvE is the correct direction.  If anything, the decision to abandon the original concept raises an interesting question:  What design problems did PvPvE solve, and could reintroducing PvE revive some of those problems?  That's a question worth investigating rather than dismissing.  ---  The precedent concerns me more than the individual feature  This is ultimately the heart of my concern.  If ARC Raiders establishes that sustained community pressure can successfully produce a fundamental genre-level accommodation, what incentive does that create for future communities?  What happens when players purchase the next extraction shooter and immediately begin demanding PvE-only progression?  Or when a survival game attracts a vocal audience that wants the survival mechanics substantially reduced?  Or when developers create an intentionally unforgiving multiplayer experience, only to face sustained demands for an alternative that removes the very pressures defining that experience?  I'm not suggesting every requested accessibility feature or optional mode represents an attack on artistic integrity. Nor am I suggesting developers should blindly ignore their audiences.  Games are interactive products, and their evolution should involve the people playing them.  But there has to be some meaningful distinction between refining a creative vision and replacing it with a more broadly marketable one.  Otherwise, we risk encouraging an environment in which developers gradually homogenize distinctive experiences to accommodate every sufficiently persistent demand.  The result may be games that appeal to more people superficially, while becoming less distinctive in the process.  And I think that's a legitimate concern for an industry that already struggles with creative risk-taking.  The troubling precedent isn't that players are asking for changes. Players have always done that. It's the possibility of normalizing the expectation that fundamental genre conventions should be negotiable whenever enough people find them inconvenient.  That raises another uncomfortable question:  If a developer advertises a game around a particular set of mechanics, and players knowingly purchase that experience, why should the preferences of people who dislike those mechanics automatically receive greater consideration than the preferences of those who actually enjoy them?  Why should preserving the intended experience be treated as stubbornness, while fundamentally changing it is celebrated as responsiveness?  I don't think those assumptions should go unchallenged.  ---  Where should the line be drawn?  To be clear, Embark has every right to experiment. The current PvE option is a test, and no permanent decision has been established. The developers have also been unusually transparent about the risks and their reasons for exploring it.  I respect that.  I also recognize that some players genuinely prefer the environmental combat, exploration, and cooperative elements of ARC Raiders over fighting other players. Their preferences are perfectly legitimate.  But legitimate preferences do not necessarily justify redesigning the fundamental experience of an existing game around them.  My concern is that we've become increasingly comfortable treating creative limitations and intentional design decisions as problems developers have an obligation to eliminate.  Sometimes a game simply isn't designed to provide the experience somebody wants.  And that's okay.  We shouldn't need every game to accommodate every possible playstyle, particularly when doing so may come at the expense of the experience other players specifically came for.  I'd be interested in hearing what people here think, especially those who approach this from a game-design perspective.  - At what point does an optional mode stop being an innocent addition and start changing the identity of the game around it? - Should developers prioritize accommodating a larger potential audience even when doing so risks diluting their original vision? - Is there a meaningful distinction between improving accessibility and removing mechanics that are deliberately central to a game's identity?  And perhaps most importantly:  «Is there still value in developers telling players, "We understand what you're asking for, but that isn't the game we're trying to make"?»  Because I think there absolutely is.  And I worry that gaming as a whole stands to lose something important if we increasingly treat that answer as unacceptable.

Ciao a tutti,Ultimamente ho letto molte discussioni sul concetto di "realismo" nei videogiochi e il consenso sembra sempre lo stesso: "Il realismo è noioso, la vita vera è già fuori, i giochi devono essere solo divertimento staccato dalla realtà".Da persona che vuole iniziare a sviluppare videogiochi, ho la sensazione che l'industria ci abbia convinti di una grande bugia: che realismo significhi solo "aggiungere compiti noiosi e animazioni lente".Quando un moderno gioco tripla A dichiara di essere realistico, cosa fa in concreto? Costringe il personaggio a fare un'animazione fissa di 5 secondi solo per raccogliere un oggetto da terra, o ti costringe a guardare una barra della fatica che si svuota mentre corri. Questo non è realismo, è solo una limitazione artificiale. Risulta legnoso e rigido perché il giocatore perde il controllo diretto e fluido sul corpo del proprio avatar \[Riferimento: Turni Precedenti\].Cosa succederebbe se ridefinissimo il "realismo" non come un insieme di divieti noiosi, ma come Libertà Fisica dei Sistemi e Interazione Naturale?Immaginate un gioco di sopravvivenza o di simulazione in cui:Il mondo fisico ha una sua vera integrità: Non rompi gli alberi a pugni perché una barra della salute invisibile arriva a zero. La tua mano rimbalza e risente del colpo a causa della densità e della fisica della materia. Per interagire devi usare leve, pesi ed energia cinetica in modo fluido, dando ai comanti un controllo assoluto e preciso, senza animazioni pre-registrate \[Riferimento: Turni Precedenti\].Il mondo sociale ha una logica emergente: Invece di avere PNG (NPC) che seguono binari scritti o che ti ignorano, le IA reagiscono a ciò che vedono basandosi su memoria e buon senso. Se un negoziante assiste a un evento bizzarro o subisce uno shock, non si limita a glitchare: la sera ne parla con altre IA al bar, cambiando organicamente l'economia locale, i prezzi e le reputazioni attraverso il puro passaparola nativo, senza una singola riga di dialogo fisso scritta da uno sviluppatore \[Riferimento: Turni Precedenti\].Se un gioco offrisse questo livello di connessione pura e reattiva con l'ambiente e la società — dove il mondo si evolve da solo per collisione di materia e di pensiero, invece che per meccaniche finte — sarebbe davvero noioso? O semplicemente non lo abbiamo mai visto fatto nel modo giusto?Sono sinceramente curioso di sapere cosa ne pensate. Se poteste cancellare tutti i cliché finiti dei videogiochi (scritte volanti, barre della vita, animazioni rigide) e li sostituiste con la fisica e la biologia naturale dei sistemi, quale sarebbe la prima interazione che vorreste testare sul campo?

Over the short history of video games, designers have learned a LOT on how to make games more universally engaging, intuitive, and overall just more fun. When we take off the rose-tinted glasses and honestly look at our time-honored classics, the mistakes of their early experimentation become painfully apparent. I wish our knowledge of modern game design principles could be imported into the past not only to rectify those mistakes, but to positively change the gaming landscape to come. Hence, the thought experiment: assuming you could send one game back in time (and the means to play it) as a model of good design, **what would be the best game to send back in time to exemplify?**    **No game is perfect**, and as such, no game is exemplary in all of its design choices. Feel free to point out aspects of the game which you believe would have revolutionized that area of game design. Also, different genres have had to solve very different problems over the years, so a very impactful game in one genre may not have much to teach in another genre. Would you want to have a far-reaching influence on all game design, or showcase the pinnacle of your favorite genre?     \----  ive posted some example of good game that wouldve benefit the gaming industry if it were send back to the past in the comment (to avoid the "no list post rules")

When you start looking, you find these suckers everywhere. Not all of the below games fit exactly, but a lot of them are close.  - SOMA - Nobody Wants to Die - Firewatch - Spectrum Retreat - Bradwell Conspiracy - Ether One - Close to the Sun - Gone Home - Deliver Us the Moon - Before Your Eyes - Hellblade (the remote woman is in your head and there are ten of them) - Relicta - Everybody's Gone to the Rapture (recordings rather than companion) - Callisto Protocol - The Station - Still Wakes the Deep - Suicide of Rachel Foster (role-reversal) - Draugen - Blair Witch 2019 - Someday You'll Return - Mouthwashing??? - Return to Grace - Beyond Blue - Subnautica Below Zero (actual gameplay here) - Superliminal  - Filament - Portal 2 (a vague cousin of this genre) - Q.U.B.E. 2 - Observation (role-reversal) - Paradise Lost - The Invincible (remote man in this one) - Edith Finch (there is a woman but she's the protagonist)  I was curious why this is such a common format, and I think it's because it's just really well suited to telling a particular kind of story on a low budget.  It's very difficult to tell a good story with just the protagonist talking to themselves, so you need at least one other character. But NPCs with body/facial animations and their own AI are difficult and costly to animate. So rather than having a companion who goes through the game with you, just have your companion be somewhere remote where you can't see them, and make them speak to you through an ear piece (or through some other means).  This choice only really comes about when the devs are aiming to create a very specific kind of game - one which is narrative driven and feels 'AA', but on a low budget, or with a small team.   If they didn't mind the game looking a bit cheap, they'd just create NPCs and accept that they might be ugly.  If they didn't actively need the narrative to drive the experience, they'd cut the companion or use text-based dialogue.  But these are games that want to punch above their weight in terms of production values and tell a serious story. They don't want to look cheap. Often, they look the opposite - they are bursting with gorgeous scenery (which is doable because beautiful scenery is a lot easier to do on a budget than NPCs).  That's also why these games rarely have combat. They might include puzzles, but most of the time, they fall back on allowing the player to look around their world, interacting with items/notes/books and listening as the protagonist and the 'remote woman' talk about them. Then, at pre-determined points, control will be taken away from the player so that we can watch a cutscene play out. Cutscenes are almost always in these games (because it helps with the production value) but they also tend to be modest or sparing (because of budget limitations). When we do see NPCs, they are often 'ghostly' looking, made of particle effects, or otherwise not made to look like real people (because that's expensive).   I'm not quite sure why it's overwhelmingly a remote *woman*. Possibly because these games are aimed at male players, and male players are more likely to want to play as a man and form an easy relationship with a female character. Possibly because the devs want a contrast. And often I think it's because they want the remote voice to provide human warmth, and women tend to deliver that better. The 'male loner and mysterious female confidant' relation works well because there's a lot of room for teasing, flirting, and emotional vulnerability.  Do you like this subgenre (if you think it counts as one at all)? Or do you think it's overdone?

I definitely haven't kept up with every single discussion, so I'm not claiming these are original ideas. You can play solo, but you don't necessarily have to be completely independent. Even a solo player could belong to a larger Stalker organization or faction.  As you gain experience and reputation, you could eventually join factions such as **Duty or Freedom**.  You wouldn't have to join one, though. Remaining an independent Stalker could itself be a viable playstyle.  You could spend your time:  * Hunting mutants * Searching for artifacts * Trading * Exploring anomalies * Taking contracts * Fighting other players * Working as a medic or courier * Playing in the Rostok Arena * Or literally just sitting around a campfire and talking to other Stalkers  Some people might play the game primarily for the social aspect.  # PvP shouldn't be like Rust  This is one of the biggest differences I'd want.  In Rust, killing someone you encounter can often be the obvious choice because there isn't much stopping you besides the immediate consequences.  In a STALKER MMO, killing another player should have **social and faction consequences**.  Imagine you're a Duty member and another player kills you for your artifacts.  Everyone in your faction could receive a PDA notification:  >**Duty member killed.**   Location: Dark Valley.   Time: 21:43.   Suspect: Unknown.  The killer might eventually be identified through witnesses, evidence, PDA information, etc.  If they are identified, they could become wanted.  A bounty could be placed on them.  Now killing someone isn't simply:  >"I got his loot."  It could become:  >"I just made an entire faction my enemy."  The potential value of the loot might not be worth the consequences.  Players could even organize hunting parties:  >"Who killed him?"   "Raven."   "Where?"   "Dark Valley."   "Let's go."  And suddenly six or ten players are hunting that person.  # Faction wars  Factions could control territories.  A faction could announce:  >**Duty–Freedom conflict**   Army Warehouses   Saturday, 21:00  This would create actual organized battles instead of random PvP everywhere.  During a faction war, players could be constantly moving around with binoculars, watching for enemy movements, setting up defensive positions, transporting ammunition and evacuating wounded players.  The war shouldn't simply be about kills.  Control of territory, supply lines, bases and strategic locations should matter.  And the important part is that **death should have consequences**.  If you die during a major faction battle, you shouldn't be able to instantly respawn and run straight back to the battlefield.  # Death and injury  I'd have two completely different states:  # Seriously wounded  You are shot and go down, but you're still alive.  Another player can find you and rescue you.  They can stabilize you, carry you out of the battlefield and take you to a medical station or faction base.  If you're rescued:  * You spend around 15–20 minutes recovering. * You keep most of your equipment. * The player who rescued you receives XP, money and reputation. * You return to the Zone relatively quickly.  This would create an entirely new role for players.  # Dead  If nobody finds you and you bleed out, you're actually dead.  Your character doesn't get deleted, but death should be a serious event.  You might lose the equipment you were carrying, while items stored in your stash remain safe.  And instead of instantly respawning, you could have something like a **minimum one-hour recovery period**.  During a faction war, this becomes extremely important.  You can't simply:  >die → respawn → return to the front line → die → repeat  A faction would actually have to manage its manpower.  Maybe a battle has:  * 20 players on the front line * 15 in the second line * 15 reserves  If the first line suffers heavy casualties, the reserves have to be sent in.  Suddenly players become strategically important.  # Medics  This could create a genuine player profession.  Someone might say:  >"I'm really good at being a medic."  Their PDA could show something like:  **Field Medic: 92**  They specialize in stabilizing and transporting wounded players.  They might not be particularly good with a rifle, but during a major battle they could be one of the most valuable people there.  If your medic dies, the whole group's ability to recover wounded players is affected.  # Tanks / heavy fighters  Another player might specialize in heavy armor.  They have:  * Heavy armor * Defensive artifacts * High physical resistance * Heavy weapons  Their job is basically:  >"I'll go first. Medic stays behind me."  They might be slow, but extremely difficult to kill.  # Logistics  Another player could specialize in ammunition and supplies.  Their artifacts might increase:  * Carrying capacity * Stamina * Endurance  Their job isn't necessarily killing people. You could develop different skills, but becoming exceptional at everything should take an enormous amount of time.  This would make every experienced player useful in a different way.  # The PDA should matter  The PDA could become the actual social and military information system of the Zone.  You could receive information such as:  >**A Duty member has been killed.**  Or:  >**Freedom convoy spotted near Yantar.**  Or:  >**Territory battle scheduled for Saturday, 21:00.**  Or:  >**Your faction member is wounded and requesting medical assistance.**  But the PDA shouldn't reveal everything instantly. You might only log in for a few hours a day, but when your faction has a major battle, you know when it is happening. This makes the faction feel like an actual organization rather than just a colored team.  # Rostok could become a social hub  Rostok wouldn't just be somewhere you pass through. A skilled player could play guitar at a campfire or in a bar.  Other players could sit around and listen.  A good performance could give:  * XP * Tips * Reputation  You could literally have a player whose entire thing is:  >"I'm the guy who plays guitar in Rostok." If you want to fight another player, you can do it there without turning the entire Zone into a KOS environment.  You could have:  * Duels * Team fights * Betting * Tournaments  If you get shot in the Arena, you wake up in the infirmary instead of losing your character.  That gives players a place to enjoy PvP without making random murder the optimal strategy everywhere else.  # Independent Stalkers  And I think this could create some amazing YouTube content. **Warning. Full Spoilers for both games below in case anyone hasn't played them yet.  And also just a precaution to anyone that I enjoyed both of these games very much. For varying reasons. So this is not coming from a place of hate.**  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------  Ghost of Yotei has one of the strangest and most confused revenge plots I've ever experienced that makes TLOU2 look like actual Shakespeare.  People mocked TLOU2 for delivering a heavy handed message that they felt was hypocritical because Ellie guns down hundreds of people throughout the game only to let Abby go at the end.  Regardless of where you stand on whether TLOU2 was good or bad. I think we can at least agree that TLOU2 fully commits to actually showing the psychological and systemic consequences of revenge.  Both Ellie and Abby's quest for vengeance is explicitly framed as a physically and psychologically damaging obsession that not only fails to bring them any emotional closure, but also gets their friends and families killed, inciting conflict between the WLF and Jackson communities that largely have nothing to do with each other.  Every faction involved that's lost a loved one believes that they have a "just cause" and feels entitled to retribution for crimes committed against them. This allows the story to hammer the point home that in this fundamentally lawless land, everyone wants an eye for an eye, but in the end, neither side gains anything of value from the senseless violence.  This is why Ellie and Abby's actions are fundamentally selfish and meaningless. The solution for both was to stop perpetuating that senseless violence and remove themselves from that never-ending cycle. Otherwise it doesn't stop.  Even if you consider it cliche or heavy handed. This is why TLOU2's revenge premise actually works.  **WHERE GHOST OF YOTEI FAILS**  Ghost of Yotei on the other hand, has a revenge premise that simply doesn't work.  GOY attempts to frame Atsu’s journey as a complex path of self-destruction on paper, but in practice, she saves Ezo from Saito and the Yotei 6.  The game tries to treat her actions as morally questionable, but because the "Yotei 6" are so cartoonishly evil, everything Atsu does is an objective net positive for the region and its people. She essentially becomes Ezo’s Batman.  The second Atsu enters Ezo, she immediately causes a massive shift in the war between Saito's force and Clan Matsumae. Clan Matsumae are essentially the local police and law enforcement (I won't get into the corrupt politics of Samurai clans and caste systems because it's not particularly relevant for the plot of GOY as it was for Tsushima).  The point is that Atsu and the local police are completely aligned in their mutual objectives to clean up the streets from a terrorist group. There is no "moral" conflict here. Atsu's presence is less of a moral grey anti-hero, and more of an objectively instrumental force of good that gives them a far greater advantage than they ever had.  Despite this. The game frequently tries to convince the player that Atsu is being selfish.  For instance, the game frames her choice to go after the Oni as reckless due to the Oni's overwhelming strength and the risk towards the captured Matsumae samurai. But Atsu is the only person to make this much progress in getting close enough to the Oni to kill him.  And while she fumbled the initial attempt. She ultimately succeeds when Juubei finally agrees to disobey his commander and follow Atsu's lead. They successfully kill the Oni thanks to Atsu.  The game tries again to make Atsu seem selfish when she later prioritizes killing the Dragon over going to the fortress with Juubei. However, the narrative clearly demonstrates that the Dragon was a dangerous master strategist, and they would never get another opportunity to take him down.  It's quite literally thanks to Atsu that they were able to draw out the Dragon which Clan Matsumae was never able to do.  By forcibly drawing him out and eliminating him on the spot, Atsu actually prevents a far worse massacre, undermining the idea that her quest is purely self-serving.  Despite this. The story chastises Atsu for doing this because Juubei and Clan Matsumae have been captured. Which in all honesty, is a bigger reflection of Clan Matsumae's own incompetence rather than it being Atsu's responsibility.  After emotionally chastising Atsu. The game then attempts to show Atsu's emotional growth through her interaction with the Spider.  We learn that the Spider suffered a lot of emotional abuse from Saito, his dad, and was forced to live up to his impossible expectations. Atsu forgives him and lets him go. The narrative expects us to view Atsu letting him go as a profound moment of breaking the cycle of revenge and violence.  However this completely falls flat because the Spider is a wonton mass murderer who has slaughtered probably thousands of civilians and Clan Matsumae members, he tortured and killed Atsu’s family and threatened to kill her niece and made a theatrical play about it.  The game unironically expects the audience to believe that "daddy issues" are justifiable enough reasons to exonerate a war criminal.  In TLOU2 when Ellie spares Abby it makes sense because Abby has already shown Ellie mercy twice already and has actively tried to end the cycle with her. By that point, killing Abby achieves nothing and only endangered Lev.  However, Atsu letting a dangerous criminal evade justice feels entirely unearned because the Spider has not done anything to prove that he has actually reformed. It is an extraordinarily contrived "redemption".  We then get to the last chapter of GOY which is titled "The Cost of Revenge", meant to further reinforce the premise of how Atsu's actions have a cost, but it hilariously fails because nothing Atsu has done in this game has "incited" revenge.  Clan Matsumae getting captured, injured or killed is not a consequence of "revenge" because this stuff was already happening irrespective of Atsu's involvement.  But anyway. So to once again use TLOU2 as a reference. Ellie and Abby removed themselves from the cycle of violence but only after facing a brutal reckoning.  Everything they lost along the way proves that their revenge wasn't worth it.  GOY attempts to replicate this tragedy by having Saito kill Atsu's brother, but this fails yet again because the game seems to frequently forget that Clan Matsumae are the police.  If a police officer gets captured, injured or killed while in the line of duty trying to stop a gang of terrorists. You cannot blame the local vigilante for this. That's ridiculous.  Juubei's death has nothing to do with Atsu. It's a natural consequence of the samurai role he took on. They are in a war against Saito. How is that Atsu's fault?  And the overall conclusion contradicts its own "revenge is bad" theme. Atsu kills Saito, fulfills her quest and saves Ezo.  Her reputation as an Onryo frightens away future threats, and the people worship her for it. The game delivered an overwhelmingly positive outcome, yet the narrative continues to awkwardly pretend that her revenge was wrong.  She made Ezo a safer and better place for her niece who doesn't have to experience what she did. And thanks to doing this, Atsu managed to also find a reason to live.  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------  **TL;DR**-   Ghost of Yotei wants to tell a story about the destructive consequences of revenge, but its actual plot completely undermines that premise by making Atsu's revenge significantly beneficial and tries to blame for consequences that aren't actually caused by her revenge.  The revenge premise in GOY is farcical. The heavy handed moral chastising the game's narrative attempts to portray falls apart when everything she did resulted in an overall net positive.  For a "Revenge Bad" narrative to work. The revenge needs to be bad. But in GOY, Atsu's revenge may as well been a divine blessing.

Resonant suffers from the same problems that have put me off a lot of recent AAA games: they never make you feel like you're in new world. Many layers of abstraction act as guardrails keeping you at a safe distance.  Anything you hit feels like you're swinging a pool noodle at a concrete block. Start up is fast, cancels are generous. There's no impact in the world or weight to the character. Instead impact is mediated by a skill tree. +X% damage if you are in the air.  They create these skill trees that are like a jigsaw puzzle meant for a five year old. Put the parts together and you get a big picture, you're supposed to play according to this scheme that came pre-assembled for you. That's because the physicality is not there.  The world is bolted to the ground, most things are static.  In Control 1 if you wanted to throw something at an enemy you needed an actual object around you to use as a projectile. You had to worry about cover and positioning in its claustrophobic environments. The destruction was super detailed.  On the other hand Control had a confusing map with a lot of backtracking, repetitive combat and an even more pointless skill tree. Though that last one's more of an advantage over Resonant for making the skill tree secondary to the combat.  But it was still a better game for me because it didn't tell me how to play it, it didn't have its entire world abstracted away by status effects and pre-arranged playstyles.  In the end I think this picture [https://imgur.com/NsdqLyu](https://imgur.com/NsdqLyu) really sums up the problem I have with Resonant and other AAA games. That's a pop up that appears as you enter a 2 minute section of walking. It's a reminder that says "hey if you feel frustrated soon don't worry okay, you are still safe and can quit".   I think this feeling was made all the more jarring to me having just played Half Life Alyx before Control Resonant, a game that's 100% about the physicality of the world. It's unfortunate AAA leans more and more in these RPG elements. Might as well make it a turn based game, I'd enjoy it more.

One thing I have always found fascinating about Horizon is that it refuses one of the easiest ways of writing a post apocalyptic world. It does not tell us that humanity was corrupted by civilization and that the answer is to return to some simpler, more authentic existence. But it also does not tell us that humanity is doomed, that every society will inevitably become oppressive and that the future can only be a darker version of the present. Its world is not a utopia, but it is not a dystopia either. It is a world made by people who inherited both the achievements and the mistakes of those who came before them.What I appreciate most is that the game applies this idea consistently to both the Old World and the new civilizations that emerge after Zero Day.  The tribes of the new world are not romanticized. Horizon never falls into the "noble savage" trope where people living closer to nature are somehow morally superior. The Nora have strict traditions that can become oppressive. The Carja have a history marked by conquest and religious violence. The Tenakth have built parts of their culture around warfare and strength. The Quen have created a rigid socety where access to knowledge is controlled by a privileged class.  These societies are not presented as perfect alternatives to the world that came before them. They are human societies, which means they carry all the contradictions that come with being human. But what makes Horizon special is that it also refuses to look down on them.  A lot of stories would have used these cultures simply as exemples of ignorance waiting to be corrected by modern knowledge. Horizon is much more compassionate than that. The player often knows that many beliefs come from incomplete interpretations of Old World technology, but the game is interested in something deeper: why do people create these beliefs in the first place? I believe it's the most important theme of HFW for the matter.  The Utaru are probably the best example. Their understanding of the world is scientifically inaccurate, but the game never treats their traditions as something ridiculous. Their rituals around death, renewal and the land exist because people need ways to understand suffering and their place in the universe. Their beliefs are not true in a scientific sense, but they are meaningful. Horizon understands something that many science fiction stories forget: humans do not build civilizations around facts alone. They also build them around stories.  The Quen storyline develops this idea in a direction I personally found to be fascinating. Their civilization is built around fragments of Old World history, especially the remains of a corporate civilization they barely understand. Their interpretation of the past is often distorted, but their mistake is not simply ignorance. What makes the Quen particulary interesting is that they have not only preserved knowledge from the Old World, they have also preserved its values. Their society has absorbed the logic of corporate hierarchy, the worship of exceptional individuals and the idea that progress belongs to great leaders rather than the countless people whose work makes it possible. Their reverence for the Ancestors reflects this distorted memory of a world where CEOs became almost mythical figures while ordinary workers disappeared from history. In that sense, the Quen are a mirror held up to our own values and to the ways in which modern societies still decide whose contributions deserve to be remembered. Such an inventive and fun way to develop a culture!   This is why I think Horizon has such an interesting view of history. The past is never simply recovered. It is constantly rewritten by the people who inherit it. This approach is very akin to what could be found in Fallout New Vegas, minus the cynicism and fatalism of it.  The high level of nuance exists in the way the games portray the Old World. The apocalypse is terrifying precisely because it does not feel like a cartoon dystopia. It does not need every corporation to become an absurdly evil caricature or every institution to openly announce its cruelty. The world collapsed because of recognizable human tendencies pushed to catastrophic extremes.  That is what makes the Old World disturbing. It feels less like a fantasy and more like a warning. I know that Horizon is doing things right when the news constantly remind me of its  events and characters.  The most frightening parts are often not the giant machines or the apocalypse itself. They are the ordinary moments where systems fail. The corporate language that turns ethical disasters into management problems (could the Timor-Hartz have been annihilated if FARO had not tried to cover up the situation with an army of lawyers ?). The obsession with innovation without responsibility. The belief that technology can fix problems that are ultimately political and human.  This is also why I think Horizon's approach to dystopia feels different from many other science fiction worlds. A lot of dystopian fiction relies on exaggeration. Corporations become almost mythical forces of evil, governments become completely absurd, and society becomes so extreme that it feels disconnected from our own reality. Horizon is much more unsettling because it does the opposite. It takes things we already recognize and asks what happens when those tendencies continue without limits. Horizon's world is not a dystopia and this makes it actually more terrifying than a dystopia could ever dream to be.  At the same time, Horizon never falls into pure cynicism. This is probably the most important part of its identity. The game shows the consequences of human arrogance, but it never concludes that humanity itself is the problem. The new civilizations are flawed, sometimes deeply flawed, but they are also capable of kindness, cooperation and change.  This is ultimately why Horizon's world works so well for me. It does not offer the comfort of a perfect future or the simplicity of a hopeless one. It understands that every civilization is built by imperfect people trying to make sense of an imperfect world.  The old world was not destroyed because humanity was incapable of creating great things. The new world is not valuable because it escaped humanity's flaws. Both worlds contain beauty and failure.  And that is exactly what makes Horizon feel alive. Forging such a complex and nuanced world is no easy feat, and filling it with rich and touching reflections on our current world is truly impressive. It is a step above something like Cyberpunk 2077, imo. I feel like these games have been mischaracterized by some people as examples of good storytelling that are still somehow below the games that are constantly showered with praise for their stories and writing. That's a shame, not because that opinion is objectively wrong, but because it has prevented some people from really delving into what the developers actually constructed. Hello everyone,  I am doing academic research as part of my **Master of Science in Strategic Management and Digital Marketing at the University of Malta**. As a gamer who enjoys studying game design and how monetisation works inside gaming, I want to better understand how the gaming community perceives and responds overall to one of the increasingly common monetisation methods nowadays, time-limited offers.  For the sake of clarity, in this survey time-limited offers refer strictly to cosmetic item offers, excluding any sort of offer/purchase that provides any sort of gameplay advantage/functional benefit.    **Purpose of the survey**  The aim of this study is to examine how time-limited offers in video games are associated with FoMO and impulsive purchasing behaviour among young adult players.  In particular, the study investigates the relationship between perceived scarcity, Fear of Missing Out (FoMO), and impulsive purchasing behaviour. It also examines whether FoMO helps explain how time-limited offers may influence impulsive purchasing decisions.  **Abstract**  This dissertation investigates how time-limited cosmetic offers in video games are associated with player perceptions, emotions, and purchasing behaviour. The study focuses on these main concepts: perceived scarcity, Fear of Missing Out (FoMO), and impulsive purchasing behaviour.     I have the following hypotheses:  * **H1:** Time-limited offers in video games are positively associated with FoMO among young adult players.  * **H2:** Time-limited offers in video games are positively associated with impulsive purchasing behaviour among young adult players.  * **H3:** FoMO positively influences young adult players’ impulsive buying behaviour.  * **H4:** FoMO mediates the relationship between time-limited offers in video games and young adult players’ impulsive buying behaviour.  To pursue the following objectives:  1. To examine the relation between time-limited monetisation mechanics and players’ perceived urgency in video game environments. 2. To assess the relationship between time-limited monetisation mechanics and video game players’ FoMO. 3. To analyse how perceived urgency and FoMO relate to impulsive purchasing behaviour toward time-limited in-game offers.     **Potential benefits**  The community may benefit from reflecting on how time-limited in-game offers affect their feelings and purchasing decisions. The study may also help increase awareness of the psychological factors involved in these types of monetisation strategies. More broadly, the research aims to contribute to a better understanding of scarcity-based monetisation, FoMO, and impulsive purchasing behaviour, and to support wider discussion around responsible in-game monetisation practices.    **Criteria to participate**  * Age: **18-35** * gaming experience: Must have played games at least once * Purchase status: Must have purchased a time-limited offer at least once    **Survey Ethics**  * The survey includes screening questions to ensure that only participants who meet the study criteria can proceed. * Participation is entirely voluntary, participants can withdraw from the survey at any point before submitting their responses. * Participation is entirely anonymous, no personally identifiable information will be collected at any stage of the survey.    If you require further information/clarification please do not hesitate to contact me via my   university email: [orestis.d.nikolaidis.25@um.edu.mt](mailto:orestis.d.nikolaidis.25@um.edu.mt)  Survey link: [https://forms.gle/ryRao1m445GJaJY36](https://forms.gle/ryRao1m445GJaJY36)     If you could share this around to people who might be interested and/or are eligible it would mean the world to me!    **Discussion**  I am more than happy to discuss the topic in the comments! I would definately be interested to hear your general thoughts and experiences with time-limited cosmetic offers in games.

Just to be upfront: I work in player research in the games industry. No product, no links, just an idea I want to discuss.  Here's my claim: what players actually value in living worlds is spectating and not cohabiting. If NPCs genuinely lived their own lives, most players would stop engaging with them within the first session.  Here's why I think that. Twenty years of autonomous NPC attempts produce the same two reactions: noticed behaviour becomes an anecdote we retell for years, and missing behaviour makes us call the world empty. Both are about being in the audience, neither requires actual interaction. Then when researchers recently dropped hundreds of AI agents into sandbox worlds and these agents formed jobs and even a religion, everyone read the articles, but nobody asked to be a part of it. There's a darker version too, where an NPC with real agency competes with you for authorship. A world that changes on its own is atmospheric until it builds something where you were going to build.  The best counterargument I can think of is that nobody has shipped real cohabitation, so players never had the chance to want it. Maybe the watching preference is just learned from decades of NPCs not being worth talking to.  That's the idea. I'd rather be wrong, so if your experience contradicts it, I'm listening.

I keep seeing "AI-generated game" and "procedurally generated game" used as if they describe the same thing. I think they answer different questions.  AI generation describes how an artifact or its code was created. Procedural generation describes what the game does with rules, usually at build time or runtime. An AI can write a completely fixed level. A developer can hand-write a seeded generator that produces millions of levels. The way something was authored does not automatically define how it behaves.  The distinction becomes clearer with four simple cases:  Human-written code, fixed map.   Model-written code, fixed map.   Human-written code, seeded map generator.   Model-written code, seeded map generator.  Only the last two contain procedural map generation. The model in the fourth case may have created the generator, but the usual procedural questions still apply: rule constraints, reachability, distribution, reproducibility, useful seeds, and whether the variation actually changes the experience.  There is a fuzzier case when a model generates new content during a play session. If the output is sampled differently each time but has no stable seed or inspectable rule system, I am not sure "procedural" fully explains what is happening. It may be dynamic content generation, but debugging and reproducing a bad result become very different problems.  My current test is simple: if the model is removed after the code is produced, does the running game still generate content from a defined procedure? If yes, calling it procedural seems reasonable. If no, the AI label may be doing most of the explanatory work.  Where do you draw the boundary for AI-generated content at runtime? Is reproducibility part of your definition of procedural generation, or just a useful property?

I've been experimenting with a different way of ranking games.  Rather than asking someone to directly rank 50 or 100 games, I have them make a series of simple choices between two games:  "Which do you prefer?"  Those choices feed into an ELO-style rating system. Games start at 1000 and move up or down depending on the result and the rating of the opponent.  The idea is that it's much easier to make a meaningful comparison between two games than to decide where an entire list of games belongs.  I ended up building a site around the idea called Omega Ranking. It produces personal rankings, GOTY lists, decade lists and an overall favourite game list.  Here's [my profile](https://omegaranking.com/Account/Profile?username=Tom&utm_source=r_truegaming) so you can see what kind of a page it builds for you.  I'd be interested to hear what other people think of this as a way of measuring someone's actual game preferences.  [Omega Ranking](https://omegaranking.com/?utm_source=r_truegaming)

So one thing I’ve noticed in gaming discussions is how selectively people appeal to consensus. If someone likes a game that has strong critic reviews and strong user scores, they’ll often be told that reviews don’t matter, popularity doesn’t matter, sales don’t matter, and they should form their own opinion which is fine on paper but the moment people dislike a game, suddenly it becomes:  “Lots of people criticised this.”   “This is a common complaint.”   “Even reviewers said the same thing.”   “Look how many people agree that it’s bland.”  You can see the problem right?  If I defended Spider-Man 2 by saying it reviewed extremely well with both critics and players and sold tons (which it objectively did), plenty of people would immediately tell me that those metrics doesn’t prove quality and I'd be shut down for appealing to them to validate my positive take on the game. Yet some of those same people will turn around and appeal to “common criticism” of Wolverine as though the number of people repeating a criticism suddenly makes it objectively true which feels completely backwards to me.  Either consensus has evidentiary value in these discussions or it doesn’t. You can’t dismiss 90% positive reception when it supports a game you dislike, then invoke “lots of people say this” five minutes later when the crowd happens to agree with you.  And I think this happens constantly in gaming discourse. People don’t really have a consistent standard for reviews, Metacritic, user scores, sales or community sentiment. They treat each one as meaningful or meaningless depending entirely on whether it helps their current argument.  Personally, I think consensus can be useful for describing how a game was received, but it obviously doesn’t settle whether any individual criticism is correct and what annoys me is pretending otherwise only when convenient...

I want to clarify first that the goal of this thread isn't to be contrarian and go against the grain on unpopular opinion. What I'm trying to do is spark civil discussion about how budget affects art, not just trying to shit on a thing that's popular.  With that being said, I'm not on the hype train for GTA VI. I'm simply not a fan of Rockstar and their games so of course I wouldn't care about the new one. I've expressed this opinion in various spaces and almost inevitably, I hear the same type of argument to defend Rockstar and explain why, seemingly empirically, GTA VI will be the greatest game of all time.  These arguments are something to the effect of "The game has a budget of over a billion dollars and has been in development for so long. Nothing on this scale has ever been made. It has to be great."  I understand the logic behind that argument as it's pretty straight forward. However, the more I've thought about it, the less it works as an argument and if anything, gives me more reason to be wary of GTA VI.  To understand why I'm wary about it, I think it's worth understanding a simple rule when it comes to pretty much all entertainment. The higher the budget, the more money it has to make back to be profitable. If an artist wants to focus on making niche things, that's great but they'll have to be comfortable with working in lower budgets, since there won't be a larger audience.  This is why a lot of fantasy novels simply can't be adapted to film or television. Gardens of the Moon is a great fantasy novel but if it were to be adapted, it would need a very high budget for all the effects, sets, costumes and etc. However, to remain faithful to the source material, it would need to be complex and hard to follow, which means it won't reach a wider audience. It's a paradox.   This is why Marvel movies get high budgets, because they're designed to appeal to as many people as possible so they're confident in making the money back.  This applies to all entertainment, including video games. Ubisoft can make repetitive slop with increasingly high budgets because they expect it to appeal to the largest audience possible.  I'm not saying that every piece of entertainment that's popular is bland. What I'm saying is that entertainment that's DESIGNED to be popular is bland and high budget makes appealing to the broadest possible audience higher on the list of priorities in development.   Grand Theft Auto VI has the highest budget of any video game. With a budget that high, this doesn't just need to be a popular video game. It needs to be THE video game, the one every gamer owns.  We know very little about the story, but I can't imagine the writing being anything worthwhile when it's meant to appeal to everybody. I'm not saying that a good story can't be popular, but I have to believe that appealing to the most people possible was a high priority during development.  Where I especially imagine the writing taking a hit is in GTA's satirical edge. Grand Theft Auto hasn't had deep political commentary, but the games have had a satirical edge when it comes to portraying modern American life. The writing was never super biting, not like it was written by Jon Stewart, but there were groups and people that you could tell the writers didn't like.  How can they maintain that satirical edge when "appealing to everybody" is such a high priority? How can they poke fun at various aspects of modern America without losing any possible players, especially in times where things feel so divided?  To give an example, the game takes place in Florida. Wouldn't it make sense for there to be a character that's an analog of Ron DeSantis, controversial governor of Florida? I could imagine it fitting very well. I could imagine a bit after a heist, a cutscene could open with characters watching the news, where the state governor gives a speech, decrying the recent string of heists as the result of anti-American protesters, with the criminals responsible smugly watching, maybe making a quip like "Heh, the only thing we're protesting is being broke", celebrating recent success.  I think it would fit. I think he's an easy target for most people. But then I remember, this isn't for most people, this is for everybody. Do you get my point?  To conclude, I do honestly hope that GTA VI will turn out great just because I know people have waited so long for it. However, I can't honestly believe that something with this high of a budget can be anything more than bland slop. I think too many people see a high budget as only a good thing, without seeing the constraints that a high budget brings to art.

Japan studio, despite its storied history, has been shut down, and that feels so unfortunately emblematic of where Sony is at these days.  My introduction to Sony was with the PlayStation 2. Xbox was for crude frat bros salivating at the jiggle physics of Dead or Alive, Nintendo pushed out quality titles that felt a bit juvenile at the time, but PlayStation was \*art house cinema\*. This was a console bursting with style and creativity. From the AAA blockbusters like Final Fantasy X and Metal Gear Solid 2; to the mascot platformers like Sly Cooper and Jak; to the wonderfully bizarre Japanese titles like Katamari Damacy and Mr. Mosquito, it was a wonderfully eclectic catalogue of games to suit all all manner of tastes. Standing proudly in the crowd was Team Ico's Shadow of the Colossus. While discourse around the artistry of games wasn't as developed back then as it is now, but this game was spoken of in hushed tones with how commanding of a presence it had with its oppressive atmosphere and unprecedented sense of scale.  Cut forward to today and that diversity of games is nowhere to be found, at least not within the halls of Sony owned studios. This isn't to slander the great work that studios like Sucker Punch, Santa Monica, and Naughty Dog have done, but when all you are putting your money behind is the triplest of AAA cinematic blockbusters, they all begin to lose their luster when sat next to each other. Sony is no longer the steward of gaming's wildest and most exciting new titles, it is a content mill of 'premium gaming content'.   This is really unfortunate, because this console generation, Sony needed teams like Japan Studio more than ever. Studios that ,while not producing the best-selling games of the year, create a much more colorful catalogue of games for people to enjoy and fill in the gaps during the 3-5 year lulls between major studio outputs. Those prestige titles are what endear customers to these companies, and that goodwill can be cashed in during times of distress. Nintendo only just barely survived the Wii U generation because their history of quality titles had the hardcore fans stick by them, and new fans eager to receive them when the Switch came out.  I am no financial analyst and don't want to make any predictions about Sony's future, but I feel that things are not looking good from a public relations standpoint right now. Team Blue has spent the past 6 years blowing enormous amounts of money and wasting studios' precious time chasing live service trends to no avail. Studios are made to bet the farm on their massive first party outings, so if one underperforms, that could spell death for their employees. With only 4 new IPs under their belt this generation, 2 have been discontinued and nothing has come to fill the gap. Strong assets like Bluepoint and Kojima productions have been let go, all the while they spurn their hardcore fans with the death of game discs. Had Sony done the work to incubate stranger, more adventurous titles from the likes of the now defunct Japan Studios, maybe it would make all these bitter pills we've been swallowing go down just that little bit easier.

By this I mean, as videogame-playing Gen X-ers and Millennials have grown up, has the mid 2000s - 2010s debate around videogames being art essentially been resolved?  To give some context, a decade and a half ago years ago late American film critic Roger Ebert [pretty famously argued (repeatedly) that video games can never be art](https://www.rogerebert.com/roger-ebert/video-games-can-never-be-art) because the player is in ultimately in charge of the camera, and not the director. And also because he considered basketball not art, video games weren't art.  A lot of digital ink was spilled, focusing on people coming up with definitions of art, talking about the prestige of what people think of as proper 'high art' and 'low art', arguments are about authorship and camera direction that can't be controlled by the director, ideas that games aren't art but composed of art, etc.  More than just the prestige, there was also legal significance in countries like the US, [where courts were deciding on freedom of speech in regards to artistic works](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/the-art-of-video-games-101131359/).  >The Supreme Court ruled last June that video games should be considered an art form, as deserving of First Amendment safeguards as “the protected books, plays and movies that preceded them.” (2012)  This was a big deal, especially given the context of the 2000s moral panic the video games in the US faced with things like Jack Thompson [arguing a link between video game violence and real-life mass shootings](https://3rdworldgeeks.com/2022/02/01/remembering-jack-thompson-video-games-greatest-villain/) and with in regards to things like [GTA's removed Hot Coffee minigame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Coffee_(minigame\)) or [media hysteria from certain news networks that claimed Mass Effect 1's sex scenes were full graphic pornography](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PKzF173GqTU).  There was (is?) also [an 'art game' movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_game), which was typically experimental, indie, non-commercial, and pushed outside of the typical understanding of video game design. And some of them like [Flower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower_(video_game\)) earned commercial success and critical acclaim. People with different sensibilities wanted games to be taken seriously, and for some creatives, that meant exploring the interactive art space.  But **it's over, right?**  Games are a bigger industry than films and music combined. Hollywood studios are now mining video game stories and settings for adaptations. The British Academy Film Awards recognizes games. The Grammys give awards to game music. Symphonies and orchestras [have been performing video game music for a decade now](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/how-video-games-are-saving-symphony-orchestras-and-filling-concert-halls/).  The only thing missing I would say is something like a [national government film registry that collects games for preservation which they consider culturally significant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Registry).  The generations that saw games as just toys or sports are dead or dying off, and there's not that same artistic impulse among game developers nowadays to "prove" that games are art. The buzz and debate in enthusiast circles also isn't about this anymore. Nobody cares, because "games are art" has won.   And so, looking back at what feels like the dead "games as art" debate, I'm going to make a historiographical claim that it had both a material influence on games (as an industry, artistic medium, and product of popular culture) and also reflected how audiences and developers were changing how they thought about games (similar to the artistic shift to grittier, more R-rated games following the runaway success of GTA3).

With the rise of remakes recently in games we got tons of many different shape and sized. Some that are just visual remakes while others are massive overhauls or reimagining  However the discussion, or rather criticism, of remakes at times boils down to how much things are different. As if for some people the only goal of a remake is being as similar to the original as possible, at times to the detriment of it being a good games for the current standards of gaming.  One example of a remake that for me it didn’t change enough was Metal Gear Solid Delta. That game was in a tricky spot where due to the very unique presentation and style of the original the creators of the remake wanted to be as faithful to the original as possible, which I agree. However I feel for a current AAA game the gameplay was pretty lacking. They made strives to have the actual controls be modernized, but everything else was almost exactly the same as the original, from boss fights to level design. For me that combination didn’t work. With the added control and speed that you could move the PS2 level design feels way more restrictive and claustrophobic, and some of the boss fights just have zero challenge, like The End, due to you being able to quickly flank, reposition and shoot.   Some might argue that they should have kept the gameplay/control faithful to the original game to mitigate this, but I feel that this remake would have been more interesting if they accommodated some of the enemy design and level design around the new movement controls. Have the maps feel much larger and free form, have the End boss be in one large area that feels like a massive arena, have the enemy AI be smarter and akin to MGSV. Have some of the map feel less like a tight corridor  So what’s like to ask is, is there a remake where you felt it should have been more different from the original for a better experience?
